About me

Munashe Thelma Chandiringa

I work where data meets decisions. Councils, mines, farms and agencies all need to know what is changing on the ground, and few have time to dig through raw imagery and spreadsheets.

I do that part. I collect and clean the data, analyse it with GIS and remote sensing, and hand back a map or report that is clear enough to act on. I’ve done it in the field at weather stations, in code with Google Earth Engine and Python, and in plain language for people who just want the answer.

Selected work

Every project starts with a real question and ends with something a decision-maker can use.

Where is Nyanga’s mountain vegetation changing, and what comes next?

QuestionPark managers needed to know where vegetation is shifting, what is driving it, and which areas are most at risk.
What I didBuilt a Google Earth Engine pipeline on harmonised Landsat 5, 7, 8 and 9 imagery (2003–2023). Measured change with kNDVI, EVI and NDWI, tested trends with Mann-Kendall, found hotspots with Getis-Ord G*, and used Random Forest to rank the drivers.
ChallengeEarly climate projections came out nearly identical across scenarios. I traced it to collinear predictors and poorly scaled sensitivity settings, re-screened the inputs (Pearson |r| ≥ 0.70) and rebuilt the outputs so each pathway gave its own result.
ResultWoodland grew from 29.8% to 54.9% of the park while shrubland fell from 48.9% to 21.7% (kNDVI, 2003–07 to 2018–23). The driver model reached R² 0.71 on held-out data, with fire frequency and night lights as the strongest drivers. Four climate pathways were projected with Monte Carlo uncertainty. This was my Honours dissertation.
  • Google Earth Engine
  • Landsat
  • Random Forest
  • Mann-Kendall
  • Getis-Ord G*
  • CMIP6

How do you give farmers data they can trust, season after season?

QuestionAgricultural advice is only as good as the weather and crop data behind it.
What I didAs GIS Intern in the Agro-meteorology section, I took synoptic observations at weather stations, captured and quality-checked station data, and tracked rainfall onset, dry spells, soil moisture and crop conditions.
ResultTwelve months of checked observations and season monitoring feeding agro-meteorological bulletins and farmer advisories.
  • Climate data
  • Quality control
  • Crop monitoring
  • Meteorological Services Department

How do you make station weather data easy to explore on any device?

QuestionRaw station readings are hard to read at a glance, especially on a phone.
What I didPrepared four spatial layers in QGIS, exported them with qgis2web, then extended the output by hand: a Leaflet map of 10 stations across all provinces, 168 hours of data across 8 weather parameters, Chart.js trend charts, a station list and a responsive layout.
ResultA working dashboard you can open and explore. It runs on simulated data to demonstrate the full QGIS-to-web workflow. Open the weather dashboard →
  • QGIS
  • qgis2web
  • Leaflet
  • Chart.js
  • GeoJSON

How can an organisation publish spatial data on the web with free software?

QuestionMaps are only useful if the people who need them can open them.
What I didBuilt a complete open-source WebGIS stack: PostgreSQL/PostGIS for the database, GeoServer on Apache Tomcat to publish layers as WMS, and MapStore as the web map client. I loaded a secondary-schools layer and published it as a shareable web map.
ResultA working path from database to web map, documented step by step in a practical write-up.
  • PostGIS
  • GeoServer
  • MapStore
  • Apache Tomcat
  • WMS

How do you count crops in a field without walking every row?

QuestionCounting plants by hand across a whole field is slow and inconsistent.
What I didBuilt a desktop tool in Python that loads a field GeoTIFF, runs a trained YOLOv8 model to find individual cabbages, and exports the results.
ResultEvery detection comes out as a georeferenced box with a confidence score, ready for QGIS or ArcGIS, plus an annotated image and a total count.
  • YOLOv8
  • Python
  • OpenCV
  • GeoPandas
  • Rasterio

Concept: “Eyes on the Ground”

QuestionSatellites show that land is changing but can’t always confirm why.
The ideaA paid youth network that verifies satellite signals on the ground, pairing field data with remote sensing. Developed for the Zimbabwe Youth Innovation HackLab 2026.
  • Field verification
